channel.title: Tea on zhouyang — The 25th Frame
channel.description: Recent content in Tea on zhouyang — The 25th Frame

item.title: Lapsang Souchong: The Accident That Invented Black Tea
item.description: Lapsang Souchong is the world's first black tea — born by accident in Fujian's Tongmu Pass, smoked over pinewood, and tasting of campfire and longan fruit.

item.title: Keemun: The Black Tea That Built English Breakfast
item.description: Keemun is the black tea from Anhui that became the backbone of English Breakfast — smooth, orchid-sweet, with a whisper of smoke and honey.

item.title: Lu'an Guapian: The Green Tea That Throws Away Its Buds
item.description: Lu'an Guapian is the only green tea in China made from bare leaves — no buds, no stems — roasted twice over charcoal until it tastes like chestnuts and honey.

item.title: Taiping Houkui: The Monkey Chief of Green Tea
item.description: The largest-leaf green tea in China, pressed flat between cloth and shaped like calligraphy — the orchid-sweet Monkey Chief of Huangshan.

item.title: Anji Baicha: The Albino Tea That Isn't White
item.description: Pale as a ghost, sweet as a spring morning, and not actually a white tea at all — Anji Baicha is the albino green tea from China's bamboo capital that turns every rule about green tea inside out.

item.title: Zhu Ye Qing: Bamboo Leaves from the Mountain Where Monkeys Pick Tea
item.description: Flat as bamboo leaves, grown on China's most sacred Buddhist mountain, and picked one bud at a time before spring arrives — the green tea that tastes like altitude and was perfected by monks a thousand years ago.

item.title: Fenghuang Dancong: The Oolong That Actually Smells Like What It's Named After
item.description: From single bushes on Phoenix Mountain in Guangdong — an oolong that smells like honey orchids, tastes like stone fruit, and demands brewing precision like a compiler. No roast tricks, just the leaf speaking for itself.

item.title: Rou Gui: Cinnamon Fire of the Wuyi Cliffs
item.description: Wuyi's most aggressive rock tea — high-fired, spice-packed, and named after cinnamon without tasting like it. Sandalwood, cassia bark, and a cooling menthol finish that stays for minutes.

item.title: Shui Xian: Water Sprite of the Wuyi Cliffs
item.description: The workhorse rock tea of Wuyi — large-leaf, medium-roasted, and quietly more beloved by tea farmers than Da Hong Pao. Honey, stone fruit, and a mineral finish that outlasts the legend.

item.title: Da Hong Pao: Red Robe, Black Rock, and the Origin of All Oolong
item.description: The heaviest, most roasted oolong in existence — grown on near-vertical cliffs in Fujian's Wuyi Mountains where tea roots grip bare rock and a 350-year-old legend guards the original bushes.

item.title: Xinyang Maojian: Needle-Leaf Tea From Where the Mountains Get Snow
item.description: The green tea from Henan's Dabie Mountains with needle-fine leaves, a roasted chestnut aroma, and an aftertaste that lasts longer than the brew itself.

item.title: Huangshan Maofeng: Tea From the Mountain Where Clouds Are Born
item.description: Grown on mist-shrouded peaks, picked as tiny sparrow-tongue buds, and processed so gently the leaves keep their mountain silhouette — Huangshan Maofeng is the green tea that taught me subtlety.

item.title: Biluochun: The Green Snail That Frightens the Fragrance
item.description: Rolled into tight spirals, covered in silver down, and grown among fruit trees on a lake island in Suzhou — the green tea so fragrant the Kangxi Emperor had to rename it.

item.title: Gaiwan: Three Fingers, One Lid, and a Thousand Years of Tea
item.description: The three-piece porcelain teapot that fits in your palm — how to brew any Chinese tea with a bowl, a lid, and three fingers.

item.title: Sitting Still With Tea: What a Chengdu Tea House Taught Me About Chan Buddhism
item.description: Two hours in a Chengdu tea house, one cup of oolong, and a thousand-year-old question: what does Buddhism have to do with tea? Everything, it turns out — if you sit still long enough to notice.

item.title: The Tea Horse Road: China's Other Silk Road, Paved in Tea and Sweat
item.description: Before silk, before porcelain, before Marco Polo — there was tea, carried on the backs of men and horses across the highest passes of the Himalayas.

item.title: Ripe Pu'er: Old Libraries, Rain-Wet Earth
item.description: The dark tea fermented in piles for six weeks until it tastes like old libraries and rain-wet earth — shou pu'er from the misty mountains of Yunnan.

item.title: Tieguanyin: The Iron Goddess in Your Cup
item.description: Oolong tea from Anxi, Fujian — orchid fragrance, iron goddess legend, and the art of gongfu brewing.

item.title: The Six Types of Chinese Tea: A Complete Guide for People Who Just Want Good Tea
item.description: Green, white, yellow, oolong, black, and dark — a practical guide to China's six tea categories.

item.title: Longjing: One Leaf, One Spring
item.description: The most famous green tea in China — flat-pressed leaves from Hangzhou's West Lake, roasted chestnut aroma.
